Source: This Is Your Brain on Music
Author: Daniel J. Levitin
Concept: Music and science as one inquiry
Source Summary: The introduction frames music as both personal experience and scientific mystery, joining listening, memory, sound, and perception.
Hearth Application: The Hearth node can explain that learning guitar is not only technical progress. It changes how the learner hears, attends, remembers, and makes meaning.
Notes: Printed page to PDF page offset is plus 6 for main text.

Source: This Is Your Brain on Music
Author: Daniel J. Levitin
Source Summary: Chapter 1 introduces core musical elements such as pitch, timbre, melody, rhythm, harmony, loudness, tempo, meter, and contour.
Hearth Application: Study should define musical vocabulary as living sound, not as dead terminology. This supports the music-as-language model: vocabulary before grammar.
Notes: Useful for beginner definitions and misunderstood-word support.

Source: This Is Your Brain on Music
Author: Daniel J. Levitin
Concept: Rhythm loudness and harmony as perception
Source Summary: Chapter 2 focuses on how listeners discern rhythm, loudness, and harmony as organized musical information.
Hearth Application: Rhythm lessons should include listening and body response, not only counting. The learner should experience rhythm as felt prediction and movement.
Notes: Strong bridge between Study and Practice.

Source: This Is Your Brain on Music
Author: Daniel J. Levitin
Source Summary: Chapter 3 explores how the mind processes music behind conscious awareness.
Hearth Application: The Hearth can use this to explain why repetition works: some guitar learning becomes automatic because the brain builds listening and movement patterns below the surface.

Source: This Is Your Brain on Music
Author: Daniel J. Levitin
Source Summary: Chapter 4 centers musical expectation and anticipation: the mind listens forward, predicting what might happen next.
Hearth Application: TeachingEngine ask moments can use anticipation: before revealing a sound or chord movement, ask the learner what they expect to hear.
Notes: Potential source for interactive listening design.

Source: This Is Your Brain on Music
Author: Daniel J. Levitin

Hearth Application: The simulator can help learners build mental shelves: chords, sounds, styles, and techniques become findable categories rather than loose facts.

Source: This Is Your Brain on Music
Author: Daniel J. Levitin

Hearth Application: The Hearth voice can safely tell learners that emotional response is not decoration. Feeling is part of how music becomes memorable and meaningful.
Notes: Good source for Hearth reflections after practice.

Source: This Is Your Brain on Music

Notes: Useful for visible intervals to mastery.
